title: Paradiski | Linked ski areas | Snow Catchers
description: How La Plagne and Les Arcs fit together across the Vanoise Express, which base reaches which side, how the snow changes with height, when the Paradiski pass pays, and what the area is like for boarders, families, food and evenings.

hero.lead: La Plagne and Les Arcs, two of the big resorts of the Tarentaise, sit on facing slopes with a deep valley between them, and since {{f:ve_opened}} the Vanoise Express cable car has carried skiers across it. The operator counts {{f:op_km}} of piste and {{f:op_runs}} runs, from the woods above Villaroger to the Aiguille Rouge at {{f:op_top}}. A single day can begin among the high apartment blocks of Plagne Centre and end on the forest runs above Peisey.

network.h2: Two resorts and one cable car
paras: Paradiski is two ski areas joined at a single point. La Plagne spreads over a high bowl of purpose built villages above Aime, with Montalbert, Champagny-en-Vanoise and Montchavin-Les Coches on its lower flanks. Les Arcs climbs from Bourg-Saint-Maurice through Arc 1600, Arc 1800, Arc 1950 and Arc 2000, with Peisey-Vallandry and Villaroger at its edges. The Vanoise Express joins Montchavin-Les Coches to Peisey-Vallandry, and in the map data it is the only lift between the two resorts.

Everything between the two halves rests on that crossing. Closing the Vanoise Express cuts {{f:ve_cut}} pairs of sectors off from each other, every journey from one resort to the other. Two more lifts matter nearly as much. Without the Peisey chair, skiers from La Plagne reach Peisey-Vallandry but cannot go on into the rest of Les Arcs, and without the Montalbert gondola none of the other {{f:montalbert_cut|w}} sectors can be reached from Montalbert by lift.

La Plagne also leans on a few lifts within its own bowl. Closing the Bijolin chair on the Montchavin-Les Coches side adds {{f:bijolin_extra}} lift rides in total across the journeys between sectors, and closing the Colosses chair at Plagne Bellecôte adds {{f:colosses_extra}}. The villages of Les Arcs are linked to each other more than one way, so a single closure there costs time rather than access.

areas.intro: The pass covers villages built for skiing high on the mountain, such as Belle Plagne and Arc 2000, and older villages lower down, such as Montchavin, Champagny, Peisey and Villaroger, whose lowest lifts start between {{f:lo.villaroger|n}} and {{f:lo.peisey-vallandry}}. Where a sector sits relative to the Vanoise Express decides how quickly the other resort can be reached.

paras: Les Arcs and Peisey-Vallandry count {{f:la_green}} green, {{f:la_blue}} blue, {{f:la_red}} red and {{f:la_black}} black runs, and La Plagne counts {{f:lp_runs}} runs, {{f:lp_blue}} of them blue. skiresort.com measures {{f:F000075}} of the piste across Paradiski as easy, {{f:F000076}} as intermediate and {{f:F000077}} as difficult.

In the map data every sector can be reached from every other on green and blue alone, and allowing reds never shortens a journey. The one shortcut is a black run from Champagny-en-Vanoise, which saves a lift ride on the way to Montchavin-Les Coches and everything beyond it: on green and blue, Arc 2000 takes {{m:easy.champagny.arc-2000|w}} lift rides from Champagny instead of {{m:all.champagny.arc-2000|w}}.

That makes the area easy to share across a group of mixed ability, on one condition: the meeting point has to be on the right side of the cable car. From Plagne Bellecôte, Arc 1800 is {{m:all.bellecote.arc-1800|w}} lift rides away; from Montalbert it is {{m:all.montalbert.arc-1800|w}}.

The steepest and longest skiing is high in Les Arcs. The run from the Aiguille Rouge to Villaroger is {{f:av_len}} long and drops more than {{f:av_drop}}, and Arc 2000 has the speed skiing track used at the {{f:la_olympic}} Olympics. In La Plagne the Glaciers gondola climbs to {{f:lp_top}} by the operator's figure, the highest point of the resort.

paras: Most of the skiing sits well above the villages. The lowest lift in Arc 2000 starts at {{f:lo.arc-2000}}, and on the elevation model the Aiguille Rouge cable car climbs to {{f:hi.arc-2000}} and the Glaciers gondola to {{f:hi.bellecote}}. The edges are low: Villaroger, Montchavin, Champagny and Peisey all have lifts starting between {{f:lo.villaroger|n}} and {{f:lo.peisey-vallandry}}.

The weather model behind the snowfall figures covers the whole area with one grid cell, so it cannot tell La Plagne from Les Arcs, but it shows plainly what height does. In a typical season between 1991 and 2020, about {{f:s1600}} of snow fell at 1,600 m, {{f:s2100}} at 2,100 m and {{f:s2600}} at 2,600 m.

The lower slopes have lost the most. At 1,600 m the typical season fell from {{f:s1600_old}} in 1961 to 1990 to {{f:s1600}} in 1991 to 2020, and every one of the last five seasons sat in the lowest third of the 76 year record. At 2,600 m the fall was smaller, from {{f:s2600_old}} to {{f:s2600}}, and two of the last five seasons were that poor.

On this evidence the high villages of either resort are the safer base in a thin winter. The calendar points the same way: the Vanoise Express and the lower sectors of La Plagne, Montalbert, Champagny and Montchavin-Les Coches, close on {{f:ve_closes|dm}}, a week before the high ground of both resorts on {{f:lp_closes|dm}}. The model gives snowfall rather than depth on the ground, and measured depths from weather stations are still being collected.

paras: A six day adult Paradiski pass costs {{f:F000066}} in high season. The single resort passes undercut it by very little: {{f:lp_6d}} for La Plagne and {{f:la_6d}} for Les Arcs and Peisey-Vallandry, savings of {{diff:F000066,lp_6d}} and {{diff:F000066,la_6d}}. Either gap is smaller than a single day on the Paradiski pass at {{f:F000065}}.

For a week the arithmetic favours Paradiski, as long as the Vanoise Express is running. It stops on {{f:ve_closes|dm}}, and in the last week of the season the two resorts can only be reached from each other by road. Les Arcs also sells a Premium version of the Paradiski pass at {{f:prem_6d}} for six days, which adds unlimited sledging, a zip line ride and a swimming pool entry.

access.h2: Getting there and choosing a base
paras: By the fastest road, Geneva airport is {{f:gva_champagny}} from Champagny-en-Vanoise and {{f:gva_arc2000}} from Arc 2000, the nearest and farthest of the villages; Lyon airport is {{f:lys_min|n}} to {{f:lys_max}} away and Chambéry {{f:cmf_min|n}} to {{f:cmf_max}}. Every route ends on the RN90 up the Tarentaise valley, and the resorts' own roads climb from Moûtiers, Aime and Bourg-Saint-Maurice.

The railway follows the same valley. This winter the Eurostar ski service from London runs as two trains with a change at Lille, and outbound on Saturdays it calls at Aime-la-Plagne, Moûtiers and Bourg-Saint-Maurice. At Bourg the Arc en Ciel funicular climbs to Arc 1600 in {{f:fun_min|w}} minutes, and passengers arriving by train ride it both ways free on the day they arrive.
access.accessNote: Road distances are the fastest route by the OSRM router on OpenStreetMap data, without traffic or snow. The ski train as reported by Seat 61; the funicular by Guide Ski. 2026/27 bus timetables have not yet been checked.
basesParas: Which side of the Vanoise Express a skier sleeps on shapes the week more than the pass does. Plagne Bellecôte is the best placed for both halves, {{f:b.bellecote.plagne-centre|w}} lift rides from Plagne Centre and {{f:b.bellecote.arc-1800|w}} from Arc 1800. Peisey-Vallandry and Montchavin-Les Coches sit at the two ends of the cable car, yet from Peisey, Plagne Centre is still {{f:b.peisey-vallandry.plagne-centre|w}} lift rides away.

The corners pay for their quiet in lifts. From Montalbert, Arc 2000 takes {{f:b.montalbert.arc-2000|w}} lift rides, and from Villaroger, Plagne Centre takes {{f:b.villaroger.plagne-centre|w}}. Arc 2000 is the base for the highest skiing, with a lift top above 3,000 m {{f:b.arc-2000.top3000|w}} rides from the village.

paras: Each resort keeps its own parks. Les Arcs has the SPARK Snowpark at Arc 1600 and a boardercross at the Col de la Chal on the Arc 2000 side. La Plagne has the Riders Nation park, the Funslope in Plagne Bellecôte, which Guide Ski calls the longest of its kind in Europe, the Buffalo Park and a lit tunnel called the Equalizer, with boardercross courses at Champagny-en-Vanoise and Montchavin-Les Coches.

Drag lifts are where the two resorts differ. In the map data {{f:m_drags}} of the {{f:m_main}} main lifts are drags. They make up {{f:drag.montalbert}} of the main lifts in Montalbert and {{f:drag.plagne-centre}} in Plagne Centre, against {{f:drag.arc-1800}} in Arc 1800 and {{f:drag.bellecote}} in Plagne Bellecôte, which makes Les Arcs and the Bellecôte bowl the easier bases on a board.

Away from the parks, the run from the Aiguille Rouge down to Villaroger is the long ride of the area, {{f:av_len}} with more than {{f:av_drop}} of descent. Terrain beyond the markers is not controlled, so the avalanche bulletin and a local guide come first.

paras: France.fr lists Montalbert and Montchavin under Famille Plus, the national label for family resorts, and both are among the lower villages of La Plagne. The Pack Famille on the Paradiski pass and the child rate for seniors help on the price.

La Plagne does most for beginners. The CoolSki areas have free lifts and marked circuits, Buffalo Kids is a play area on the snow for children, and Belle Plagne has a Family Spa with an outdoor pool at 35°C. The bobsleigh track built for the {{f:lp_olympic}} Olympics, the only one in France, takes passengers in winter.

Les Arcs has learner areas in Arc 1800, Arc 2000 and Vallandry, with the Piste des Minis in Arc 1800 and the Forêt des Pitchouns in Vallandry for the smallest skiers. The Luge 1800 and the Luge 2000 sledging runs are included without limit on the Premium pass, and Arc 1800 has the swimming pool, La Piscine.

For a base, Plagne Bellecôte has the highest share of green and blue in the map data, {{f:easy.bellecote}}, and sits within easy reach of both resorts; Guide Ski finds the most services and activities of the Arc villages in Arc 1800.

paras: Paradiski has no Michelin star in the 2026 guide, and its pleasures are terraces and the farm cooking of Savoie rather than tasting menus. Between Belle Plagne and Champagny, the Roc des Blanchets has a south facing terrace reached on gentle blues. On the Bellecôte side the Chalet des Colosses, with a red British phone box outside, is known for its vegetarian dishes as well as its fondue, and Les Inversens near the top of the Roche de Mio has a terrace big enough for large groups.

Lower down, the Chalet de la Roche in Plagne 1500, at the foot of the bobsleigh track, is the stop for pizza, and the Chalet du Friolin at the bottom of the Bauches lift in Montchavin sets out deckchairs on its terrace.

Les Arcs has the more storied tables. Belliou La Fumée occupies a hunting lodge built for Victor Emmanuel of Italy and cooks over a fire, and Les Chalets de l'Arc in Arc 2000 bakes its own bread. L'Ancolie, in the hamlet of Nancroix, is reached with a guide on the off piste Rosset route and left by shuttle bus. Down in Le Pré, La Ferme serves fondue at the end of the run from the Aiguille Rouge.

paras: The loudest afternoon is at La Folie Douce, at the top of the Villards gondola above Arc 1800 since {{f:folie_opened}}, with an open air show from two in the afternoon and DJs from three until five.

In Arc 2000, El Latino Loco is the liveliest bar, with live music and fajitas, and Red Rock serves burgers. Arc 1950 has The Wool Sock's Pub on the snow, and Le Carré is the club for dancing until morning.

La Plagne's evenings are spread across its villages. In Plagne Soleil, Monica's Pub sits beside the Bergerie lift with a big sunny terrace, live music and DJs. In Plagne Centre, Igloo Igloo has live music and DJ sets and Bar Fort Colorado stands by the Colorado chair, while La Mine Bar in Plagne 1800 is an English style pub with live sport.

fit.catches: The catches come from the shape of the area. Everything between the two resorts hangs on the Vanoise Express, which stops a week before the season ends, and from the corners the far side is a long day away: Montalbert to Villaroger takes {{m:all.montalbert.villaroger|w}} lift rides. The older sectors of La Plagne lean on drag lifts, and the lower villages have lost the most snow, with all of the last five modelled seasons at 1,600 m in the lowest third.

compare.h2: The other large areas of Savoie
paras: Set against its neighbours, Paradiski is second in size only to Les 3 Vallées, with {{f:F000071}} of piste against {{f:F000002}} and about a fifth fewer lifts. Its day ticket costs the same as Tignes Val d'Isère's, {{f:F000065}}, and its six day pass less than either Les 3 Vallées or Tignes Val d'Isère.

Paradiski starts lower than Tignes Val d'Isère, at {{f:F000073}} against {{f:F000082}}, and tops out lower, at {{f:F000074}} against {{f:F000083}}. Its grade split is close to that of Les 3 Vallées, and in the weather model it has a little more snow at 1,600 m than either Les 3 Vallées or Tignes Val d'Isère. Les Sybelles is cheaper and snowier at that height but tops out at {{f:F000092}}.

items.dd: The three resorts the operator names, La Plagne, Les Arcs and Peisey-Vallandry, split into the ten sectors that a skier meets on the ground. Sharing the pass is recorded separately from being linked by lift and piste.

A sector counts as linked only when a route of lifts and pistes reaches it in the OpenStreetMap data. Drag lifts run one way and gondolas may be ridden down. The Vanoise Express runs two cabins on parallel tracks and is counted as one lift. A link is critical when closing one lift on it cuts routes that no other lift replaces. Tignes, La Rosière and Sainte-Foy-Tarentaise are left out of the model. The model has not yet been checked against the official 2026/27 piste map.
Operator and measured figures are both shown and never averaged. Mapped piste from OpenStreetMap is used only to compare sectors and grades.
The four areas compared use the same source for each row, so a figure can be set against its neighbour.

method.conflicts: skiresort.com counts {{f:F000072}} lifts across Paradiski, while Guide Ski gives {{f:lp_lifts}} for La Plagne and {{f:la_lifts}} for Les Arcs and Peisey-Vallandry. The elevation model puts the Aiguille Rouge cable car at {{f:hi.arc-2000}} against the operator's {{f:op_top}}, and the Glaciers gondola at {{f:hi.bellecote}} against {{f:lp_top}}. The mapped piste comes to {{f:m_km}}, against {{f:F000071}} on the listings. The modelled snowfall at 1,600 m is {{f:s1600}} on this page, while an earlier run for the same grid cell gave a slightly higher figure, and the difference is being checked. This page names each source alongside its figure.
method.sources: Research of 24 October 2026. Size, runs and resorts: Paradiski. Lifts, runs, season dates, parks and passes: Guide Ski for La Plagne, Guide Ski for Les Arcs, La Plagne lift passes and Les Arcs lift passes. Measured size and grades: skiresort.com for La Plagne and Les Arcs. History and the Vanoise Express: Wikipedia on La Plagne, Les Arcs and the Vanoise Express. Network, bases, routes and lift heights: a graph of {{f:m_lifts}} lifts and {{f:m_sections}} piste sections from OpenStreetMap (© OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL), with heights from the Copernicus 90 m elevation model via Open-Meteo. Snowfall: ERA5 reanalysis via the Open-Meteo historical weather API (CC BY 4.0). Road distances: OSRM. Facts from operators, measurements, model results and estimates are kept apart in the research files, and conflicting figures are listed above rather than averaged.
